https://www.thetimes.com/article/why-the.title: Why the slogan T-shirt is back for 2023
https://www.thetimes.com/article/why-the.text:
When the designer Katharine Hamnett went to No 10 to meet the prime minister Margaret Thatcher back in 1984, her clothes did the talking. Wearing a T-shirt that said “58% don’t want Pershing” was a radical act that firmly put the slogan tee on the map; Hamnett went on to become the grande dame of the genre, with other slogans including “Stop war, Blair out” and “Education not Trident”.
Fast forward a few decades and slogans are back (again). This isn’t the first time — over the past few years we’ve had performative luxury feminism, random French words and “wellness irony” (see Taffy Brodesser-Akner’s skewering of “kale” culture in her book Fleishmann Is in Trouble), among other slogan trends — but in a world of pithy, Instagram-first one-liners, it’s no surprise that saying it with a T-shirt is big news once more.
Especially so if you’re a celebrity. Take Hailey Bieber, for instance, who showcased her (not so) hidden sarcasm towards the current conversation about celebrity nepotism with her “Nepo Baby” cropped T-shirt last month. See also Hilaria Baldwin who responded to the charges of involuntary manslaughter brought against her husband, Alec, in the only surefire way to go viral — by wearing a sweatshirt emblazoned with the word “Empathy” while berating the assembled paparazzi.
We exist in a world where catchy captions have become saturated trends in their own right, as we meme ourselves into viral oblivion (check out @OverheardLA on Instagram, which recently posted an obituary for tired internet phrases such as “Felt cute, might delete later” and “I’m not crying, you’re crying”. ) Yes, everyone’s a copywriter now, so why not stick it on a T-shirt?
Designers who have long relied on the slogan to communicate a message that a well-cut skirt or suit cannot, have been instrumental to the revival. Recent examples go from Sacai’s “I got a feeling I’m gon’ be alright” to Raf Simons’s “Let’s drink the sea and dance” via Vetements’ “Stop being rich”. At the men’s fashion weeks last month, Acne Studios styled a tiny cropped T-shirt reading “Greta” with the top of a pair of lacy pants peeking up from stained baggy blue jeans (the reference, apparently, was Garbo, not Thunberg). Meanwhile, the designer Mike Amiri, who is of Iranian descent, took his bow wearing a simple black T-shirt emblazoned with the protest line “Woman, Life, Freedom” in solidarity with the human rights movement of the country, and Stella McCartney has collaborated with the Japanese artist Yoshitomo Nara to produce “No war” and “Stop the bombs” tees and hoodies with whimsical cartoon figures. High-ranking nepo babies can even buy a version of the “Rock royalty” top McCartney and Liv Tyler wore to the 1999 Met Gala.
Whether the topic is a human rights movement or social commentary, the new slogan T-shirt is most effective when it combines style and substance. If the Noughties had Toby Mott’s “Yoga Kills”, the Instagram age has the artist Babak Ganjei whose paintings of lines including “I’m so scared of being found out and I’m not even sure what I’ve done” do a roaring trade online. Sure beats “Live, laugh, love”.
Nevertheless, Goopy positive affirmation culture is still doing strong trade. Ganni declares “You’re gonna love it”; Anine Bing demands followers “Embody your truest form”, while Paradised gives you “Optimist”. Hilaria Baldwin’s top was from the Mayfair Group, which bills itself as “an empowering digital community . . . It’s not just merch, it’s a movement.”
But for those of us who remember slogan T-shirts in a pre-internet world, this next gen may feel slightly spurious. Henry Holland, who found fame with his tongue-in-cheek fashion designer T-shirts (“Do me daily, Christopher Bailey”) thinks that the Noughties “were the last time you went to a party and weren’t there to be seen or to get content”. His T-shirts started as an in-joke between friends to wear to the cult Hoxton club night Boombox. “I wonder if because everything is now done so much for the outside world and not just your inner circle, the by-product is that it all becomes a little bit more contrived.” A case in point: Mrs Bieber, after being papped in a car park in her “Nepo Baby” T-shirt, was seen minutes later in a different, blank top. “Life seems to be just for the picture,” muses Holland.
Certainly, it is the original slogan tees that remain the most compelling. A fact that was compounded when Vivienne Westwood died last year and the image of her draped in the words “Be reasonable, demand the impossible” went viral. For Westwood, T-shirts were a canvas for her iconoclastic ideas. From the first incarnation of her Kings Road shop she used provocative phrases to communicate her ideas; evolving from the shock factor of “Perv” and “Scum” to her personal pin-badge “I Love Crap”.
Does the spirit of Westwood still exist? The more politically inclined sloganeers can take heart: even the Just Stop Oil protesters have merch. Indeed, at the cutting edge of protest, the offerings from the cult London streetwear king Sports Banger include T-shirts with the simple line “Solidarity with Striking Workers”, as worn by the actress Samantha Morton. The brand regularly donates to UCU and RMT strike funds, and sends £5 Greggs vouchers with sales of the tee to be used to take tea and snacks to local picket lines. Jonny Banger, who helms the rave and resistance project, says: “You can caption all you want but if there is no action attached it’s just words. Our T-shirts are a by-product of a bigger idea. Heart and passion are key and if there’s none of that it’s all air. Action and co-ordination are what we need.”
See also Black & Beech’s feminist pieces, worn by Erin O’Connor; for every purchase of its “A mother’s place is in the resistance” top, £5 goes to support the Abortion Support Network. Meanwhile, Hamnett is still at it with her Choose Love T-shirt, worn by everyone from Oprah to Julia Roberts, which supports refugees.
The new slogan era? It’s serious but with added lols. Or as Banger says: “We have fun with it, which can confuse people. But if you don’t laugh, you’ll cry.”

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/music/a.title: Chumbawamba’s Dunstan Bruce: ‘After the Brits we struggled to ever get on television again’
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/music/a.text:
Dunstan Bruce got knocked down, but he’s well on his way to getting up again. Sipping a Tetley drink in the lounge of his stylish Brighton terrace, this former singer in the anarcho-communist pop collective Chumbawamba casts back nearly 26 years to their unexpected 1997 global hit Tubthumping and the lightning flash of chaos that ensues when a bunch of real-life anarchists stormed the mainstream’s barricades. The shocking talk-show pronouncements. The bucket of ice water tipped over a smug politician. The swift cultural excommunication.
“We had a great time doing all that stuff,” Bruce says with a chuckle. He is unrepentant about his bandmate Danbert Nobacon drenching John Prescott at the Brits in 1998, but well aware of the career-shortening effect of authentic prime-time rebellion. “We shot ourselves in the foot by doing it.”
His home encapsulates the dilemma of the political pop insurrectionist made famous — and financially secure — by a radio-friendly drinking song that launched a million hen-do congas. Above his fireplace a poster of punk queen Patti Smith gazes down accusingly, while in a cabinet of pop culture bric-a-brac sits a toy gorilla that sings: “He drinks a whisky drink, he drinks a vodka drink.” It’s a moral struggle at the heart of Bruce’s brilliant documentary I Get Knocked Down — seven years in the making — in which he casts himself as a “washed-up, retired radical”, angry, adrift and politically impotent as “the end times” approach.
“In my early fifties I took a bit of a dive,” the 62-year-old says of his uncreative post-Chumba lull, “wondering what I was doing with my life. I felt directionless.”
Haunted and harangued for selling out his political ideals by the ghost of the hit — in the form of the baby from the Tubthumper album sleeve, dressed in Bruce’s trademark brick-pattern suit — he creates an unflinching exposé of the post-fame mindset. Success appears particularly ill-suited to a band from Leeds’s 1980s anarcho-punk squat scene, where they muddled their way through their own “almost cult-like” concept of anarchism in a shared house in Armley. “People immediately jump to the thing that [anarchy] is no rules, it’s just chaos,” Bruce says. “In fact, it was so structured. We were getting up ridiculously early to bake our own bread.”
As ardent activists, though, they caused their fair share of mayhem. Weekends were spent hunt sabbing, liberating animals or glueing up cash dispensers on anti-apartheid demos. The police would raid their squat over anything from missing dogs to suspected terrorism. “We all got held for a couple of days at Leeds police station because they said somebody had planted a homemade bomb outside Barclays bank. That was quite a sobering experience.”
On stage, inspired by their love of northern club turns, the eight-piece band would dress up as nuns, Elvises and game-show hosts, at odds with the intense barrages of their agit-punk peers. “The theatre thing turned our shows into celebrations rather than confrontations,” Bruce says. “It felt more like a party.” As anthemic anarcho-pop provocateurs, Chumbawamba built a solid underground following, using their music to confront lying politicians, bigotry and charity rock hypocrisy while “always trying to be the thorn in the side”.
Their 1986 debut album was titled Pictures of Starving Children Sell Records. Later songs concerned the Baader-Meinhof Gang, Tiananmen Square and the 1956 Hungarian Revolution. Their 1994 breakthrough album, Anarchy, came adorned with a cover image of close-up childbirth.
By 1997, though, after their eighth album, Tubthumper, had been rejected by their independent label, this rabidly anti-establishment band had signed to EMI “to talk to more people”. They went to No 2 in the UK and No 6 in America, having shifted 800,000 Tubthumping singles in the UK. They argued that the song was a comment on the resilience of ordinary people, but was there any guilt that Chumbawamba’s big hit was so . . . un-subversive?
“Not so much guilt,” Bruce argues, “but a lot of people take the essence of the song and just identify with that. We’ve had right-wing politicians [use the song]. [Nigel] Farage used it once. When he had that plane crash [in 2010], he used it in his campaigns after that.”
To compensate, Chumbawamba “spent two years trying to f*** everything up by making radical political statements”. On a US discussion show, band mouthpiece Alice Nutter claimed that the band wouldn’t mind if fans shoplifted their records, prompting Virgin Megastores to start stocking them behind the counter. They championed Mumia Abu-Jamal, an activist battling a conviction for the murder of a Philadelphia police officer, which Bruce claims “preceded all that [Black Lives Matter] stuff about police corruption, police brutality”. The $70,000 they earned from a General Motors advert was donated to a campaign to publicise General Motors’ own environmental impact, and they turned down “just short of a million dollars” for a Nike ad.
“There were so many offers coming in, some of those decisions were quite easy to make,” Bruce says. It was just as simple, he says, to refuse a recent request to use one of their tracks, probably Tubthumping, in Clarkson’s Farm. “I guess maybe we could have taken that money and given it to a women’s refuge.”
The controversy peaked at the Brit awards in 1998. After a performance of Tubthumping during which Bruce berated New Labour mid-song, Nobacon spotted a loaded ice bucket at Prescott’s table and promptly emptied it into his face. Today, Bruce calls the prank “hilarious”, but also “the most unpopular thing we did”. Fellow left-wingers like Billy Bragg criticised them, while The Mirror arranged for Nobacon to get a bucket of water in the face himself. Chumbawamba was deemed too dangerous, opinionated and unpredictable for pop’s “old boys’ club” and their brief rampage through the mainstream was effectively over.
“People still laugh about the Prescott thing and go, ‘That was brilliant,’ ” Bruce says. “But it did change everybody’s opinion of us as a sellable product. We struggled to ever get on any other television programmes. It scared people off.”
He’s still no Blair fan, but, after 12 years of Tory rule and the internal demonising of Labour’s left, 1998 now “seems like a golden era” to Bruce. He’s relieved that the Tories are “finally eating themselves to death”, but is dismayed at recent anti-protest legislation and doesn’t have any faith in Keir Starmer as a people’s saviour. “I don’t think Keir Starmer is the person to reverse those things,” he says. “When there’s a two-tier NHS, he’ll just accept it.”
Having left Chumbawamba when they transformed into a folk outfit in 2004, Bruce ultimately emerged from his post-band slump with forays into film-making. After making a documentary with Sham 69 in China, he was filming a Levellers club tour when the crusty band invited him to join them for an encore of Tubthumping each night. Rediscovering his purpose on stage, he began writing again, formed a new band called Interrobang?! and started touring a one-man show, Am I Invisible Yet?
“Doing Interrobang?! became the answer to ‘What do I do?’ ” he explains. “It totally re-energised me.” Likewise, I Get Knocked Down: “The film became part of my recovery . . . I’ve come through the other side and found a voice again.”
Although he is wary of fame, Bruce remains “really proud” of Chumbawamba’s mainstream invasion. “Somebody might see the film and think, ‘OK, they made some mistakes and it blew up in their face.’ But the idea of taking a leap in the dark is really important.” Meanwhile, in the age of Extinction Rebellion and Just Stop Oil, it’s become a very Chumbawamba world out there.
Regarding “the kids who chucked the soup” over Vincent van Gogh’s Sunflowers at the National Gallery in October, he says: “I saw myself doing exactly that, saying those words. Those young idealists inspire me massively.” He considers the handcart again, the road to hell. “Maybe there is hope in the younger generation because we’ve created a f***ing monster.”In selected cinemas to March 28, with more dates to be added, musicfilmnetwork.com

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.title: Susanna Reid: ‘I don’t feel the need to be polite on air’
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.text:
Reid was born and grew up in Croydon, south London. She was educated privately and read politics and philosophy at Bristol University. She began her career in radio and has worked in news for more than 25 years, hosting BBC Breakfast for 11 years before moving to ITV’s Good Morning Britain, where she has been the lead presenter since 2014. She lives in south London with her three sons, Sam, 20, Finn, 18, and Jack, 17.
My first alarm goes off at 3.40am — I’ve been getting up at this time for the best part of 20 years, doing breakfast television. My three boys split their time between myself and my ex. The brilliant thing about my job is that so much of my working day is when they’re still sleeping and I’m already at home by the time they’re back from school or work.
From the moment I get up everything is calibrated to the second because I’m on countdown to being on air at 6am. I give myself five minutes to scroll through my emails and the headlines before my second alarm goes off at 3.45am. I hop out of bed, brush my teeth, throw on a coat over my pyjamas and jump in the waiting car.
I read the papers on the way, along with the briefs of all the interviewees and stories that the researchers and producers have worked on overnight. The most important thing is the Grid, the piece of paper that has the timings and key talking points for the programme. It’s a lot to absorb in the 25 minutes it takes to get to the studio in west London.
I have my first coffee at 4.25am and during hair and make-up I continue reading. At 5am the overnight editor comes into my dressing room along with whoever I’m co-presenting with that day, whether it’s Richard Madeley, Ed Balls, Rob Rinder, Martin Lewis, Ben Shephard or Adil Ray. As Bruce Forsyth used to say when I did Strictly Come Dancing in 2013, “You’re all my favourites.”
I don’t tend to have breakfast before I go on air but I’ll have some sliced apple with sunflower-seed butter during an ad break. Comfort breaks and wardrobe changes must be carefully timed. Once when I was on air my dress was too tight, so the zip broke. I had to maintain my composure before rushing off to get changed.
My highlight of 2022 was interviewing Boris Johnson at Downing Street after four and a half years of him refusing to be on the programme. This was after he famously avoided our reporter Jonathan Swain at a dairy plant before the 2019 election campaign by ducking into a fridge.
We’re good humoured on GMB but we aren’t afraid to be combative. I was infuriated when I had Sam Johnson, the Just Stop Oil spokesman, on the show. He claimed we never talked about climate change, only to then admit he never watched the show. We regularly tackle the environment and our meteorologist Laura Tobin has written a book about it. I don’t feel the need to be polite and I’ll come out fighting if a guest is being illogical.
After the show ends at 9am I go home and try to have a nap for a couple of hours. Lunch is at about 1pm and I’ll have something healthy like grilled fish and veg.
I always cook a fresh meal like lasagne or a roast for my boys at the end of the day, which is an important bonding time for me. While I’m cooking I’m getting new briefs through and I have a catch-up with my editor later in the evening.
My mornings are intense with the adrenaline of live news, so switching off is hard. I’m perfectly happy with my own company — I talk to people all day, I have a terrific team and I love my close-knit family. When the boys leave home, I know that’s going to be challenging.
In the evening I like gentle TV, nothing gruesome. A bath is a must, it completely de-stresses me. On a good night I switch the lights off at 10pm and I’m asleep within minutes.
Good Morning Britain is on weekdays from 6am on ITV1 and ITVX
Best advice I was givenJust accept that you’re going to get things wrong
Advice I’d giveLet people make their own choices — don’t impose your beliefs on them
What I wish I’d known How lucky I was that social media wasn’t around when I started
author: Sarah Ewing
